speeches.Abraham Ward Jr:
Eleven tackles a game, every game, for 236 games.

Abraham Ward Jr plays in the Green Bay secondary, and his stat line reads like a linebacker's. He has made 2,653 tackles and picked off 33 passes along the way. He has never been credited with a sack or a forced fumble. He does not rush the passer and he does not strip the ball. He finds the ball carrier and puts him on the ground, snap after snap, season after season.

The Packers made him a champion in Y79, when they beat the Chiefs 44-6 in Super Bowl CXXXVIII, and the league named him Defensive Player of the Year. One ring and one award can look like a small haul for a career this long. The tackles tell the rest of the story.

He crossed into the Hall in Y82 with another full season on his card, and he is still out there adding to the total. Abraham Ward Jr, welcome to the Hall of Fame.
speeches.Akiem Bouye:
Akiem the Dream was there at the beginning.

Akiem Bouye arrived in the real-roster era, when imported NFL stars set the league's first marks, and he started his career by winning Rookie of the Year. Then he kept going for 273 games.

He caught 1,237 passes for 10,212 yards and 131 touchdowns. At about 8.3 yards a catch he was never a deep threat, and he did not need to be. He was the chain mover, the tight end a quarterback looked for on third down and near the goal line, with a 73-yard catch to prove he could still run away from people when the opening was there.

The Chargers won four titles in those early years, in Y10, Y11, Y14 and Y15, and Bouye has four rings to match. He finished his career where he made it, in a Chargers uniform. Akiem the Dream, welcome to the Hall of Fame.
speeches.Amani Bryant:
The best quarterback never to win a ring.

Amani Bryant played 416 games, a career long enough to watch whole dynasties rise and fall around him. He threw for 79,121 yards and 763 touchdowns, and he protected the football like it was borrowed: 62 interceptions on 13,029 attempts, roughly one every 210 throws.

Then there were the legs. Bryant ran for 2,292 yards and 124 touchdowns, a quarterback who finished drives himself whenever the end zone came into view. Defenses had to account for his arm and his feet on every snap, for more than four hundred games.

He won a league MVP. He never won the last game of a season. Bryant is one of the stars who never played for the coach who collected most of this league's trophies, so he spent his career trying to beat that coach's teams instead. The ring never came. The respect always did.

Amani Bryant, welcome to the Hall of Fame.
speeches.Bilal Tolbert:
No individual trophies. Four rings. And a sack record nobody has caught.

Bilal Tolbert played 210 games at linebacker and did every job the position asks for. He made 937 tackles, about four and a half a game. He intercepted 13 passes and forced 8 fumbles. And his 22 career sacks are the most in league history, a mark that still stands.

There were no MVP votes, no Defensive Player of the Year award and no Super Bowl MVP. Tolbert never needed them. He collected four rings in the Chargers' early title years, the linebacker who was in the right place on first down, second down and third.

He began in Seattle and finished his career as a Charger. Both teams got the same player: steady, versatile and always near the ball. Bilal Tolbert, welcome to the Hall of Fame.
speeches.Cairo Asanjh:
Some players chase records. Cairo Asanjh chased Ian Finney.

They called him The Prophecy, and for more than a decade he delivered on it. Asanjh caught 1,642 passes for 27,508 yards and 280 touchdowns in 250 games, almost 17 yards a catch. He stretched defenses deep, and he held on to the ball while doing it: nine fumbles in his entire career.

He won in Seattle, and then he won again in Baltimore. Nine rings, three MVPs, two Offensive Player of the Year awards and two Super Bowl MVPs. Three MVPs as a receiver tells you how much of the offense ran through him.

He finished his career in Baltimore, still within sight of the mark set by the league's first superstar. He never caught Finney. He built a career few receivers will ever touch. The Prophecy, welcome to the Hall of Fame.
speeches.Charlie John:
Seven straight Super Bowls. Charlie John was there for every one of them.

CJ was the tight end in the middle of the Bills dynasty, seven titles in a row from Y27 to Y33, LXXXVI through XCII. Dennis Baylon went 7-for-7 in Super Bowls in that stretch, and John's ring count matches him exactly, as do Tyrone Baugh's and Rob Lowe's. That was the core. He was part of it.

He caught 840 passes for 9,980 yards and 150 touchdowns in 197 games. More than one catch in six went for a score, which tells you where the ball went when Buffalo got close. He was not there to stretch the field. He was there to finish drives, and he finished a lot of them. He even took home a Super Bowl MVP of his own.

Twenty yards short of 10,000 for his career. Nobody in Buffalo cares. CJ, welcome to the Hall of Fame.
speeches.Dan Mosley:
2,658 tackles from a defensive back. Read that again.

Dan Mosley played in the secondary like a linebacker who had wandered back to cover. Over 248 games he averaged more than ten tackles a game, a number most run stoppers never touch. And he still found the ball in the air, with 37 career interceptions. A hitter and a ballhawk in the same Lions jersey.

He did it in the Modern era, a decade of three-peats and title runs. Detroit was never the team lifting the trophy, and Mosley arrives without a ring. What he does have is a Defensive Player of the Year award, the most heavily weighted honor in this league's Dominance formula, worth twice as much as a ring.

Nobody had to tell ball carriers where Dan Mosley was. They found out. Dan Mosley, welcome to the Hall of Fame.
speeches.Dennis Baylon:
Seven trips to the Super Bowl. Seven rings. Not one loss.

Dennis Baylon was the quarterback of the Bills dynasty, and from Y27 to Y33 Buffalo did not lose on the final Sunday of a season. The Iron Island completed 75.7 percent of his passes over 253 games, the kind of accuracy that turns a playbook into a metronome. He threw for 69,448 yards and 779 touchdowns against 134 interceptions, and when the field got short he kept it himself, running in 81 more scores.

The league remembers him for one word: clutch. Four times he walked off the Super Bowl field as its MVP, and he collected three regular-season MVPs along the way. Charlie John, Tyrone Baugh and Rob Lowe each matched his seven rings, and the Bills went 113-6 in the regular season across those seven years.

He took his final snaps as a Charger. Buffalo still claims him. The Iron Island, welcome to the Hall of Fame.
speeches.God Johnson:
He changed his name to God. Then he earned it.

Mason Earl III walked into the league as a receiver. God Johnson walked out as the standard every receiver gets measured against. Some people thought the name was a joke. Defensive coordinators never laughed.

36,005 receiving yards. 378 receiving touchdowns. Ten rings, from Miami to the Vikings dynasty, and five Super Bowl MVPs, because when the lights were brightest the ball found him. And three fumbles. In his entire career. Ian Finney's career receiving mark stood for decades until God took it, with Jackson Wardell Kline lined up beside him.

There is not much left to say about a man who named himself after the only being with a better résumé. God Johnson, welcome to the Hall of Fame.
speeches.Ian Finney:
The first superstar. The Infinity Man.

Before the dynasties had names, there was Ian Finney. He was the first player in this league who made you stop what you were doing to watch, the receiver every kid in the backyard pretended to be.

He started with the Commanders' four-peat, then carried the Buccaneers through the Waller–Finney era with Tyrion Kline at his side: nine rings, four in Washington and five in Tampa Bay. He caught 1,902 passes for 32,980 yards and 292 touchdowns at 17.3 yards a catch, and every one of them looked effortless. Add five Offensive Player of the Year awards, an MVP and three Super Bowl MVPs.

Every great receiver who came after him was chasing Ian Finney. Most of them still are. The Infinity Man, welcome to the Hall of Fame.
speeches.Jackson Wardell Kline:
Tyrion Kline's son did not live in anyone's shadow. He built his own.

Jackson Wardell Kline grew up with a famous name. His father stood beside Ian Finney through the Waller–Finney era, and the son could have spent a career being introduced as somebody's kid. Instead he won six Offensive Player of the Year awards, one more than Finney himself.

He piled up 28,331 receiving yards and 289 touchdowns in 237 games, close to 120 yards a game. He lined up beside God Johnson in the Vikings dynasty, when every receiver in the league was measured against two names, and Kline made it three: eight rings, a league MVP and a Super Bowl MVP of his own.

He broke in with the Giants, won it all again and again in Minnesota, and finished his career in Miami. The Kline family now has a second chapter worth telling, and this one is all his. Jackson Wardell Kline, welcome to the Hall of Fame.
speeches.Jahmyr Gibbs:
Mr. Incredible was here at the start, and he set the bar high.

Jahmyr Gibbs arrived with the real-roster era, when imported NFL players set the league's first marks, and he made the Dolphins backfield his own. He carried 2,443 times for 16,644 yards and 307 rushing touchdowns, 6.8 yards a carry. Then he caught 689 passes for 4,816 yards and 115 more scores. Defenses had to find him on every snap, in the backfield or out in the flat.

He was not tidy. 140 fumbles says so. But a back averaging nearly seven yards a carry gets the ball back, and Gibbs kept giving his coaches reasons to hand it over: 422 total touchdowns, four rings and a Super Bowl MVP.

Miami was his home, and he retired a Dolphin. Every running back who came later was measured against the numbers he put up first. Mr. Incredible, welcome to the Hall of Fame.
speeches.Jakeem Friend:
Linemen do not win trophies. Jakeem Friend won seven rings instead.

For most of his career he was a Seattle Seahawk, a fixture up front through the Modern era. He has played 252 games and been credited with 526 blocks, two a game, every game, without a single MVP or Player of the Year award to show for it. That is how the job works. The reward is a quarterback who gets up clean and a running back who finds the hole where it was supposed to be.

The last four seasons have come in New York, with the Jets from Y79 to Y82, and two of those rings were won there. The jersey changed. The job did not, and Seattle still has first claim on him.

Seven rings, 526 blocks, and almost no headlines. Jakeem Friend, Seahawks legend, welcome to the Hall of Fame.
speeches.Jason Macleone:
One look at Scary Jerry and you understood the name.

Jason Macleone was imposing before he ever threw a pass, and then he threw 9,970 of them. He completed 67 percent for 73,799 yards and 771 touchdowns, with just 128 interceptions across 331 games. He took 86 sacks and never lost a fumble. When he did tuck it and run, he made it count: 71 rushing touchdowns.

His defining day came in Y78, when he quarterbacked the Vikings past the Broncos 33-27 in Super Bowl CXXXVII. Two rings, three MVPs and a Super Bowl MVP in all, and he is still slinging it in Seattle, where every new start adds to the case.

The league's line of great quarterbacks runs from Lamar through Gooden, Waller, Baylon, Brandson and the Wilson brothers. For now, it ends with him. Scary Jerry, welcome to the Hall of Fame.
speeches.Jayon Queen:
Two Defensive Player of the Year awards. Only one other player in this league has ever matched that.

Jayon Queen made 2,838 tackles in 274 games. That is more than ten a game, every game, for a career long enough to outlast most coaching staffs. For a defensive back it is not a stat line, it is a warning. He was the hitter in the secondary, the player who got to the ball carrier first and usually finished the play alone.

And he could cover. Forty interceptions say quarterbacks tested him often enough to regret it.

Queen spent his career with the Jets and never won a ring. He was one of the great stars who never played for the coach who built this league's dynasties, which meant he spent his Sundays on the other side of them, making every champion earn it. FOV, welcome to the Hall of Fame.
speeches.Juwann Gilman:
Thirteen seasons in Arizona, and almost twelve tackles every time he takes the field.

Juwann Gilman has spent his whole career with the Cardinals, from Y73 to today. In 229 games he has made 2,743 tackles and intercepted 32 passes. He has never been credited with a sack or a forced fumble, because that was never the job. Gilman works in the open field, where one missed tackle becomes six points, and he almost never misses.

He won his ring with the Cardinals in Y73, and the league later named him Defensive Player of the Year. In the seasons since, he has kept the same address and the same assignment: find the ball and finish the play.

He arrives under a stricter standard. The bar is now Career Legacy 7,500, and Gilman is the first player to clear it. Juwann Gilman, welcome to the Hall of Fame.
speeches.Kalif Suh:
A Jets linebacker since Y76, and the middle of that defense has rarely moved without him.

Kalif Suh has played 210 games and made 638 tackles, with 17 interceptions, 20 sacks and 10 forced fumbles. That is a linebacker who does a little of everything: about three tackles a game, a takeaway when an offense gets careless, and pressure when the call comes to go get the quarterback.

He won three rings in New York, in Y77, Y80 and Y82, all on Dorren Skura's teams. When Skura left for Atlanta, Suh stayed, and he has kept the Jets defense steady ever since.

He arrives under the higher bar of Career Legacy 7,500, the second player inducted under it after Juwann Gilman. Kalif Suh, welcome to the Hall of Fame.
speeches.Lamar Jackson:
The league never had to explain who he was. He was just Him.

Lamar Jackson arrived with the imported rosters of the Real-roster era, and the early marks were his to set. Over 345 games he threw for 71,958 yards and 682 touchdowns, then ran for 7,939 more yards and 95 scores. That is 6.2 yards a carry from a quarterback. Defenses could cover every receiver on the field and still lose to the man taking the snap.

He was not careless with it either: 141 interceptions on 9,885 attempts, roughly one every 70 throws. His longest pass went 84 yards. His longest run went 79. Either way, the play was never over until he was down.

Four MVPs and two rings. Baltimore was home for the heart of it, and he finished his career in Green Bay. Him. Lamar Jackson, welcome to the Hall of Fame.
speeches.Levante Hopkins:
The quiet one who did the dirty work.

Levante Hopkins never looked the part. Glasses off the field, soft-spoken in the locker room, the guy you would mistake for a team analyst. Then he put the helmet on, and nobody in the league wanted to be the one assigned to him.

He played 291 games and caught 1,194 passes for 12,353 yards and 174 touchdowns. He won nine rings and was Super Bowl MVP twice. He was the tight end at the center of the Titans' three-peat from Y70 to Y72: blocking on first down, finding the soft spot on third, and finishing in the red zone.

He never asked for the ball. He just made it hard to lose with him on the field. Levante Hopkins, welcome to the Hall of Fame.
speeches.Lloyd Queen:
Some linemen hunt quarterbacks. Lloyd Queen hunted everybody else.

Queen was Rookie of the Year right out of the gate, and then he spent 283 games proving it was no accident. He finished with 1,364 tackles, nearly five a game, a staggering total for a man lined up on the defensive line. Eight sacks and a single interception tell you his job was never the glamour work. He took on the run, filled his gap and made the play in front of him, game after game.

He never won a ring. He never won Defensive Player of the Year. There were no Super Bowl MVP trophies on his shelf. He got here on volume and staying power alone, which is the hardest way in.

Tampa Bay fans remember the Buccaneer who was always around the ball. Now the Hall of Fame will too. Lloyd Queen, welcome to the Hall of Fame.
speeches.Lukas Russell:
The Running Man started fast and never slowed down.

Lukas Russell was Rookie of the Year in his first season and retired a Seahawk 271 games later. In between he caught 1,675 passes for 24,547 yards and 265 touchdowns. That is 14.7 yards a catch over a career that long: deep enough to make safeties back up, steady enough to keep the chains moving.

He played in the Ikarras era, when Rondale Ikarras was taking every rushing record in the book, and he still found room to collect four Offensive Player of the Year awards and eight rings. Then there is the trophy that settles a lot of arguments. Russell won a regular-season MVP. Ikarras, with all those records, never did.

Fifteen fumbles in 1,675 catches. Quarterbacks trusted him with the ball, and he gave it back to them in the end zone. Running Man, welcome to the Hall of Fame.
speeches.Malakai Sawyer:
Some backs have a great season. Malakai Sawyer keeps having them.

He has played 280 games and carried the ball 2,636 times for 19,129 yards, better than seven yards a carry, with 341 rushing touchdowns. He catches it too: 235 receptions for 1,871 yards and 60 more scores. Two Offensive Player of the Year awards say the league noticed.

It started in Tennessee, where he was Rookie of the Year on the Titans team that won it all in Y72. Seattle came next, then the Jets, where he won a second ring in Y77 and ran for 212 yards in a single game in Y78, a record that stood until Y85. Four seasons in Atlanta followed, and then the road led back to New York, where he is still carrying the ball.

Malakai Sawyer, welcome to the Hall of Fame.
speeches.Michael Wilson:
Wayne's brother, and nobody's afterthought.

Michael Wilson broke in with the Ravens, made his name with the Giants and finished as a Titan. He was a pocket passer in the purest sense: 413 rushing yards in his entire career, because he never needed to run. He completed 72 percent of his passes over 214 games for 58,992 yards and 690 touchdowns, more than three touchdown passes a game.

Six MVPs. Six rings to go with them. There was one exception to the no-running rule, and it was near the goal line, where he kept it himself and scored 36 rushing touchdowns on only 101 carries.

His prime ran through Baltimore and New York in the years of Ikarras and Brandson, while his brother Wayne's name rested on durability. Michael's career ended as a Titan, cut short by injury, and the numbers he left behind still hold up against anyone's. Michael Wilson, welcome to the Hall of Fame.
speeches.Mose Junior:
Some players chase rings. Mose Junior chased ball carriers.

He made his name with the Rams, one of the stars who never wore the colors of the dynasties that ran this league. He spent his career trying to stop them instead. Mose Junior never won a ring. He did not need one to get here.

He made 2,862 tackles in 247 games. That is 11.6 a game from a defensive back, a number that belongs to a linebacker. He was a hitter first and always, the player who arrived at the ball carrier before anyone else in the secondary. And he took the ball away too: 35 interceptions over his career, plus a Defensive Player of the Year award.

The Hall is not only for the men who won the last game. It is also for the ones who made every game harder to win. Mose Junior, welcome to the Hall of Fame.
speeches.Nick Bolton:
One of the originals, and he never stopped tackling.

Nick Bolton came into this league with the imported NFL rosters of the Real-roster era, the players who set the first marks before the league started making its own stars. He played 253 games and finished his career a Minnesota Viking.

He was the complete linebacker. 1,233 tackles, close to five a game. Seventeen interceptions and eighteen sacks, almost a perfect split between dropping into coverage and coming after the quarterback. He forced exactly one fumble in his whole career, which says something about how he played: wrap up, put the man on the ground, line up again.

Three rings. No individual awards. Just 253 games of showing up and doing the job, which is its own kind of greatness. Nick Bolton, welcome to the Hall of Fame.
speeches.Pharoah Hunter:
The other receiver in the Vikings dynasty was never anybody's second option.

Pharoah Hunter broke in as Rookie of the Year and spent his prime in Minnesota, where God Johnson and Jackson Wardell Kline were rewriting the receiving records. Hunter did not need the spotlight to matter. He caught 1,523 passes for 23,261 yards and 260 touchdowns in 233 games, a little over 15 yards a catch, with a 70-yarder to prove he could take the top off a defense.

Four Offensive Player of the Year awards say the voters noticed. Four rings say the Vikings won with him. Twice he was the best player on the field on the biggest night of the year, with two Super Bowl MVPs.

He finished his career in Seattle. Minnesota remembers a receiver who made a stacked offense even harder to stop. Pharoah Hunter, welcome to the Hall of Fame.
speeches.Ray Waller:
Never count out a man whose nickname is a promise.

Ray Waller threw the ball downfield and dared you to stop it. He completed 5,510 of 7,388 passes, nearly 75 percent, for 70,128 yards and 749 touchdowns, and his 9.5 yards per attempt tell you how far downfield he liked to live. The 214 interceptions were the price of attacking. He took only 57 sacks and never lost a fumble in 278 games.

Waller was the quarterback of the Buccaneers' golden run alongside Ian Finney and Tyrion Kline. Tampa Bay won five titles in his era, and Waller has five rings and five MVPs to match, plus two Super Bowl MVPs. The two Super Bowls that got away went to his great rival, Kyric McQuay.

He won in Tampa, and he retired in Tampa. The deep ball was his signature, and the comeback was his name. Ray Comeback Waller, welcome to the Hall of Fame.
speeches.Rondale Ikarras:
Flashy, loud, unstoppable, and he knew it. He was that guy.

Rondale Ikarras never just ran through a hole. He ran through it with style, pointed at the crowd, and made sure the cameras got his good side on the way to the end zone. The Prodigal Son played like every snap was a highlight reel, and most of them were.

23,178 rushing yards. 374 rushing touchdowns. Nine rings, four Offensive Player of the Year awards and five Super Bowl MVPs. The career rushing records carry his name. He won three straight titles in Seattle, then built his legend in Baltimore, where five more rings came with the Ravens, and took one last ride with the Jets before hanging it up.

Zero regular-season MVPs. He will tell you about that one. Rondale Ikarras, Ravens legend, welcome to the Hall of Fame.
speeches.Sherman Brandson:
The General never flinched.

Six-foot-seven, built like a tank, and calm enough to put a defense to sleep before he broke its heart. Sherman Brandson stood in the pocket like it belonged to him, and for twenty seasons it did. Pass rushers came in waves and bounced off. Fifty sacks in 315 games. Most quarterbacks give that up in a few bad years.

The numbers read like a typo: 91,463 passing yards, 1,150 touchdown passes, eight MVPs and ten rings, four of them with the Super Bowl MVP trophy in his hands. He looked more like a linebacker than a quarterback, and he played like a man who knew exactly how the next five plays would go.

He did not celebrate much. He did not need to. General Sherman, welcome to the Hall of Fame.
speeches.Tyler Pacheco:
Tyler Pacheco never needed the big play. He needed the ball, and he got it.

Over 290 games the Packers tight end caught 1,384 passes for 10,749 yards and 124 touchdowns. That is under eight yards a catch, the profile of a target who lived in the short middle of the field, where the hits come fast and the catches have to be made anyway. He was a volume player in the best sense. Nearly 1,400 receptions is a career's worth of quarterbacks deciding he was the safe throw.

He won Offensive Player of the Year once and collected four rings. And he lasted: 290 games, one fewer than Levante Hopkins, at a position that wears players down.

He was never the flashiest name on the field. He was the one who was always open. Tyler Pacheco, welcome to the Hall of Fame.
speeches.Tyrone Baugh:
Seven seasons, seven championships, and Tyrone Baugh has a ring for every one of them.

He was the linebacker at the center of the Bills dynasty, the defender who did a little of everything and all of it well. In 158 games he made 656 tackles, intercepted 15 passes, sacked the quarterback 21 times and forced 11 fumbles. Most linebackers are run stoppers, pass rushers or cover men. Baugh was all three, with a habit of taking the ball away.

Dennis Baylon got the headlines on offense. Baugh's defense made sure the Super Bowls were rarely close: a 40-7 rout in Y30, the Commanders 14 in Y32, a 46-14 win in Y33. When it was over, Baugh, Baylon, Charlie John and Rob Lowe each walked away with exactly seven rings.

He never won an individual award. Seven rings will do. Tyrone Baugh, welcome to the Hall of Fame.
speeches.Von Horsted:
Fifteen seasons, one team, and a tackle on almost every series.

Von Horsted has spent his whole career in the Rams secondary, from Y70 to today. In 254 games he has made 2,658 tackles, better than ten a game, and picked off 33 passes. Like the best tacklers in this league's defensive backfields, he has never been credited with a sack or a forced fumble. His job is simpler and harder: find the ball carrier and bring him down.

The league named him Defensive Player of the Year once. He has never won a ring, and he never chased one somewhere else. He stayed in Los Angeles and kept stacking tackles, and his Y84 season, 231 more of them, carried him across the line.

He is still playing, and the all-time tackle list is within sight. Von Horsted, welcome to the Hall of Fame.
speeches.Wayne Wilson:
Four hundred thirty-one games. Nobody in this league has played longer.

Wayne Wilson's greatest weapon was simple: he was always there. Season after season he lined up under center while the league turned over around him, and the numbers piled up behind him. 90,450 passing yards, 913 touchdown passes and a 67 percent completion rate. That yardage total sits barely a thousand yards behind Sherman Brandson's 91,463.

He was no scrambler, with 1,811 rushing yards across all those games, but near the goal line he handled it himself: 88 rushing touchdowns on just 324 carries.

He won five MVPs, four rings and a Super Bowl MVP across stops with the Chargers and the Bills, and with his brother Michael he gave the league's long line of great quarterbacks its Wilson brothers chapter. He finished his career in Buffalo, still standing.

Durability is a skill. Nobody had more of it. Wayne Wilson, welcome to the Hall of Fame.
speeches.Zander Kolar:
Some defensive linemen are measured in sacks. Zander Kolar was measured in tackles.

He played 261 games up front and made 1,278 of them, close to five a game from a spot on the field where most players settle for two. The sack total stayed modest at 19, and that was never the point. Kolar lived at the line of scrimmage and ended running plays before they had a chance to become anything. Two forced fumbles and a lone interception round out a stat line built on repetition rather than flash.

Tampa Bay was home, and he arrives here with four rings. He never won an MVP or a Defensive Player of the Year award, and he never seemed to need the voters. Running backs knew exactly where he was. Offensive coordinators spent his whole career drawing up plays that went somewhere else.

Zander Kolar, welcome to the Hall of Fame.

seasonStories.tagline: One more title in green, then the coach walked out the door and the league traded everything that wasn't nailed down.

articles.headline: The Last Dance in New York
articles.dek: The Jets went 15-2, beat the Eagles in Super Bowl CXLI and handed Dorren Skura another title. Then the coach took the keys to Atlanta.
body: The Jets did what the Jets do under Dorren Skura. They finished 15-2, ran the bracket and beat the Eagles in Super Bowl CXLI. The final was 46-8. It was another Super Bowl title for the coach and New York's third in a seven-season run that also delivered CXXXVI in Y77 and CXXXIX in Y80.

The engine was Kane Van Oxley. The Ox added 145 catches, 2,496 yards and 39 touchdowns across 20 games in Y82, took the MVP and climbed into the S tier of the skill grades. Ty Lock threw for 4,909 yards and 61 touchdowns and walked off with the Super Bowl MVP. A first-year receiver, Vyncint Heath, caught 85 balls for 1,592 yards and was named Offensive Player of the Year. Up front, Jakeem Friend collected ring number 7.

Then the map changed. Before Y83 kicked off, the coach moved to the Falcons and took Van Oxley, Ryland Maxwell and Chance Woodrum with him, sending Malakai Sawyer back to the Jets. A wave of three- and four-way trades followed: Lock to the Giants, Van Oxley on to the Bears, Heath and Shareef London to Atlanta, Drake Wise through Atlanta and on to the Ravens, Dan Stout to New York.
One offseason was all it took to break up a champion. This is the story of the Y82 season, the last title of the Jets era, and the scramble that came after it.

articles.headline: Atlanta Calling, Then the Shuffle
articles.dek: The coach took three champions south and kept two. When the trades stopped, the Falcons were Heath, London, Maxwell and Woodrum, and The Ox was a Bear.
body: It started with the coach. Dorren Skura walked away from the champion Jets for the Falcons and took three of his title core with him: Kane Van Oxley, Ryland Maxwell and Chance Woodrum. Malakai Sawyer went the other way, back to New York.

That was only the opening act. Before a down of Y83, the league erupted in three- and four-way trades and Atlanta's haul changed shape. Kane Van Oxley, the reigning MVP, never played a game in red: he was flipped to the Bears. Drake Wise, brought in from the Giants for an unnamed quarterback, was a Falcon just long enough to be moved on to the Ravens. In came Vyncint Heath from the Jets and Shareef London from the Bears.

So the coach's first Falcons are Heath, London, Maxwell and Woodrum. Maxwell, 2 rings in 56 games and 1,430 rushing yards in Y82, is the back. Woodrum brings 3 rings and 931 tackles to a brand new secondary. London, 2,849 yards and 37 touchdowns in 86 games, gets a fresh start with a contender.
For Van Oxley it is pure whiplash: a title, an MVP, a ticket to Atlanta and then Chicago, all in one offseason. For Atlanta it is a reset built around the two Jets who stayed with their coach.

articles.headline: Champions Nobody Recognizes
articles.dek: The Jets kept the trophy. The coach, the MVP, the Super Bowl MVP and the Offensive Player of the Year all left. This is who is left to defend it.
body: Count what is gone from New York: Dorren Skura to Atlanta, Van Oxley to Chicago, Lock to the Giants, Heath to the Falcons, Maxwell and Woodrum with the coach. Half the roster that hung the CXLI banner has scattered.

What stays is the spine. Jakeem Friend, 7 rings and 526 blocks, still anchors the line. Jaylen Conklin, the tight end known as “Takeoff” for a vertical that lets him snatch anything thrown above his head, brings 4,502 yards and 66 touchdowns. Kalif Suh forced 4 fumbles in Y82 and sits at 10 for his career. Trequan Roberts, 2 rings, and rookie Dwayne Skura hold the secondary.

The new faces are familiar ones. Dan Stout takes over at quarterback, and Malakai Sawyer comes home: a Jet from Y76 to Y78 and a champion in Y77, he ran for 1,169 yards and 26 touchdowns for the Falcons last season and returns with 13,041 career rushing yards.
It should feel strange in New York this year. The banner is fresh, the faces are not, and Stout, ringless in 264 games, has just been handed a team that knows how to win one.

articles.headline: Three Quarterbacks, Three New Homes
articles.dek: The Super Bowl MVP is a Giant, the Ravens' starter now runs the champions' offense, and Drake Wise was a Falcon for exactly one trade.
body: Ty Lock leaves New York with 2 rings, 2 MVPs and a Super Bowl MVP from CXLI. His career line reads 22,189 yards and 239 touchdowns in 93 games, and the multi-team deals sent all of it to the Giants. Lock walks out a champion, the rare player who leaves on top.

His replacement is a volume passer still hunting a first ring. Dan Stout has thrown for 48,796 yards and 472 touchdowns in 264 games without one, and his Y82 in Baltimore added 3,055 yards, 26 touchdowns and only 4 interceptions. Now he inherits the defending champions, and with them the one thing his career has never had: a real shot at a ring.

Drake Wise took the strangest route. The coach traded an unnamed quarterback to the Giants to bring him to Atlanta, and the league-wide shuffle moved him on to the Ravens before he took a snap there. He arrives in Baltimore with 2 MVPs, 45,968 yards and 467 touchdowns, and like Stout, no ring. His Y82: 3,331 yards, 33 touchdowns, 3 interceptions.

articles.headline: The Ox and Starscream
articles.dek: Kane Van Oxley played his way into the S tier. Vyncint Heath played his way onto the map in 17 games.
body: Van Oxley's Y82 was a highlight reel in numbers: 2,496 yards on 145 catches, 17.2 a catch, with 39 touchdowns. That is a touchdown on more than a quarter of his receptions. They call him “The Ox” for the strength that breaks tackles and holds up blocks, and no player Skura has coached has recovered more fumbles. The market caught on this year: his value went from 716 to 1,515, up 111.6%. He now carries 14,921 career yards, 147 touchdowns and 3 rings to Chicago, a Falcon for a moment and a Bear for real.

Heath was the surprise. In his first 17 games he caught 85 passes for 1,592 yards, 18.7 a catch, won Offensive Player of the Year and a ring, and debuted with a skill grade of A−. They call him “Starscream”. The multi-team trades sent him to Atlanta, so he still plays for the coach who watched him break out, now beside Maxwell and Woodrum.

articles.headline: The Other Side of the Ledger
articles.dek: Not every stock went up. Two veteran receivers lost their bite and the market cooled on two defenders.
body: Juawan Lance has 4 rings and 15,422 career yards, but his Y82 season added 396 yards on 45 catches. That is 8.8 a catch for a receiver who averages 13.2 over his career. Craig Whitney caught 85 balls and turned them into just 442 yards, 5.2 a catch against a career 9.9, and his skill grade slipped to C−.

On defense, Darrel Longa logged 95 tackles in 17 games, yet his OVR dropped from 75 to 73 and his market value fell 22.5%. Taywan Tuttle's value dropped 43.5% without a new game played, the steepest fall on the market this season.
None of it erases a career. It does show which way these careers are trending.

articles.headline: Record Watch: Jensen Closes In
articles.dek: Trequan Jensen is one big season from Rondale Ikarras. The tackles race has a new name in it.
body: Ikarras holds the league's career rushing mark at 23,178 yards. Trequan Jensen sits at 21,690, 1,488 short, after a Y82 that added 1,390 yards and 19 touchdowns. One more season like that leaves him knocking on the door. He already has more career rushing touchdowns than anyone in league history, 388 to Ikarras's 374.

The tackles record belongs to Mose Junior at 2,862. Dan Mosley has 2,658 and added none in Y82, and Abraham Ward Jr has pulled to 2,653, right on his heels. Mosley also has 37 interceptions, 3 behind Jayon Queen's 40.
Kalif Suh forced 4 fumbles in Y82. That puts him at 10 for his career, one behind Tyrone Baugh's league-best 11.

articles.dek: Kirk Lenoir joined the 50,000-yard club, Ward Jr joined the Hall of Fame, and Jakeem Friend kept collecting jewelry.
body: Kirk Lenoir crossed 50,000 career passing yards with a Y82 that added 3,386 yards and 37 touchdowns. He now sits at 51,978, though his skill grade dipped to D+ on the way. Jason Macleone keeps climbing too: 73,799 yards, 771 touchdowns and 331 games, fourth on the career passing list.

Abraham Ward Jr passed 2,500 tackles and crossed Career Legacy 7,000, which makes him the Hall of Fame's Y82 class. The Packers defensive back has 2,653 tackles and 33 interceptions in 236 games, a Defensive Player of the Year and a ring.

articles.headline: Same Opponent, Different Uniform
articles.dek: Three Super Bowls against the Eagles, three wins, with three different clubs.
body: Philadelphia keeps finding Dorren Skura on the biggest stage, and it keeps ending the same way. He beat the Eagles 36-28 in CVIII with the Ravens in Y49, 38-11 in CXXXI with the Titans in Y72, and again in CXLI with the Jets. That is three meetings and three wins, each in a different uniform.

The thread runs through Malakai Sawyer. He was Rookie of the Year on that Y72 Titans team, the only season he ever spent in Tennessee, and he is the man the Jets got back when the coach left for Atlanta. If the Eagles get there again, they will meet a fourth Skura club: the Falcons.

articles.headline: Where Are They Now: The Ones Who Walked
articles.dek: Alvin Tufele retired, Dylan Hyatt left the league and Blair Iupati never played a down in green.
body: Before Y82 the Jets let two champions walk out the door, and a third never really arrived. Dylan Hyatt was not brought back and left the league. Alvin Tufele was let go too and has since retired. Blair Iupati came over from Seattle in a trade and was shipped on to New Orleans almost as soon as he landed.

Tufele came over from Seattle in the Obinna Leary trade, played Y81 for the Jets and is done: 230 games, 1,158 catches, 18,352 yards, 188 touchdowns and 3 rings. Hyatt leaves with 6 rings, 1,713 tackles and 231 games, his last club the Jets.
Iupati was a Jet for about as long as a trade call lasts. The Seahawks defensive back, 112 games and a ring, went on to the Saints before he ever suited up in New York.

seasonStories.tagline: A new club, a new quarterback, a new receiver in full flight, and the old champions waiting in the final.

articles.headline: Year One in Atlanta Ends With a Ring
articles.dek: The Falcons went 12-5, ran the table in the playoffs and beat the Jets 40-25 in Super Bowl CXLII. Dorren Skura's first season in red ended against the club he left.
body: Nobody gave the Falcons a bye. They finished 12-5, played their way in through the first weekend of the playoffs and did not lose again, finishing 40-25 over the New York Jets in Super Bowl CXLII. It was another title for Dorren Skura, won in his first season with a new club, against the champions he had coached a year earlier.

The offense belonged to people who were not in Atlanta a year before. Brandon Jaclyde, in his first 21 games in the league, threw for 5,199 yards and 56 touchdowns and was named Most Valuable Player. Vyncint Heath, the receiver they call "Starscream", turned a trade into the best season of his young career: 137 catches, 2,504 yards, 34 touchdowns and the Super Bowl MVP. Ryland Maxwell ran for 1,919 yards and 25 scores and won Offensive Player of the Year.

The defense was new too. Simeon Otton was Rookie of the Year at linebacker, Jashaun Fleming worked the line, and Trysten Floyd joined Chance Woodrum in the secondary. Woodrum, one of the three champions who followed the coach south, now owns 4 rings.

On the other sideline stood the club Skura built. Malakai Sawyer and Jaylen Conklin carried the Jets back to the final, and lost to Skura on Super Bowl Sunday, as New York has every time the two have met in the final.

The celebration did not last long. Before the second season in Atlanta began, Shareef London went to Tampa Bay for Shawn Milne, Jaclyde was traded to the Dolphins and Perrion Randall to the Seahawks. The champions are already a different team.

articles.headline: Jaclyde: One Season, One MVP, One Ring, One Trade
articles.dek: Brandon Jaclyde threw 56 touchdown passes in his first 21 games, won the MVP and the Super Bowl, and was a Dolphin before his second season began.
body: A year ago the quarterback question in Atlanta was a revolving door. Drake Wise came and went in a single trade, and the Falcons opened Y83 with a passer who had never taken a snap in the league. Brandon Jaclyde answered it emphatically.

In 21 games he threw for 5,199 yards and 56 touchdowns, about two and a half scores a game, and took the league's Most Valuable Player award. His 26 interceptions say he never stopped taking shots, and with Heath running past people, most of those shots landed. He also ran it in 4 times.
The skill grades rate him in the A band already. The market is slower: his card opened at a value of 19, a long way below the established passers he outplayed.

Then the business side arrived. Before the Falcons' second season, Jaclyde was traded to the Dolphins. Miami gets a reigning MVP with one season on his card, and Atlanta goes looking for its third starting quarterback in three offseasons.

articles.headline: Starscream Takes Flight
articles.dek: Vyncint Heath caught 137 passes for 2,504 yards and 34 touchdowns, then took the Super Bowl MVP. His skill grade climbed to A+.
body: Last season "Starscream" was a promising rookie with 85 catches on a loaded Jets roster. This season he was the reason defensive coordinators lost sleep.

Heath played all 21 Falcons games and caught 137 passes for 2,504 yards and 34 touchdowns. That is 18.3 yards a catch on a season's worth of volume, and a touchdown on roughly one of every four receptions. When the Falcons needed one more play in Super Bowl CXLII, it went his way, and so did the game's MVP award.

Two seasons in, he has 2 rings, an Offensive Player of the Year award and a Super Bowl MVP. The skill grades moved him from A- to A+, and his card value jumped 262 percent. The ceiling is not in sight yet.

articles.headline: Maxwell Carries the Load, and the Hardware
articles.dek: Ryland Maxwell ran for 1,919 yards and 25 touchdowns, won Offensive Player of the Year and added a third ring.
body: Ryland Maxwell was one of the three champions who followed Skura out of New York, and he made the move look like a promotion. In Atlanta he was the every-down back: 1,919 rushing yards and 25 rushing touchdowns across 21 games, plus another 10 catches out of the backfield.
The league noticed. Maxwell was named Offensive Player of the Year, the first individual award of his career beyond his Rookie of the Year trophy, and the Super Bowl win gave him 3 rings in 77 games.

The market has been slower to catch up. His skill grade sits at C+ and his card value of 20 is modest for a back with his resume, which makes him one of the better bargains on the board heading into the second Atlanta season, where he remains on the roster.

articles.headline: The Rest of the Roster Nobody Knew
articles.dek: A rookie of the year at linebacker, an S-grade lineman and a tight end who scored on almost a quarter of his catches.
body: Champions are remembered by their stars, but this Falcons team was built out of first-year cards. Eric Raimann caught 54 passes for 792 yards and 13 touchdowns at tight end. Perrion Randall was credited with 58 blocks in 21 games on the line and debuted with a skill score of 99, the top of the S tier.

On defense, Simeon Otton made 94 tackles at linebacker and was named Rookie of the Year. Jashaun Fleming matched him with 94 tackles and added 3 sacks up front. Trysten Floyd made 62 tackles, picked off a pass and forced a fumble in a secondary anchored by Chance Woodrum, who added 117 tackles and a fourth ring.
Every one of them now has a ring in his first season. Not all of them will wear red in the next one: Randall was traded to the Seahawks before the second Atlanta season.

articles.headline: Beating the Team He Built
articles.dek: The defending champion Jets made it back to the Super Bowl with Skura's old core. Skura has still never lost a Super Bowl to New York.
body: The Jets did not collapse after the coach left. With Dan Stout running the offense, Malakai Sawyer back in green and Jaylen Conklin still catching everything thrown above his head, New York returned to the final. Sawyer ran for 1,844 yards and 37 touchdowns, Conklin added 122 catches for 908 yards and 9 scores, and Kalif Suh made 54 more tackles.
It was not enough. The Falcons won 40-25, and Skura stayed unbeaten in Super Bowls against the Jets, now with yet another club.

The market still rated the losers' season. Conklin's card value rose 313 percent, the biggest jump in the league, even as his skill grade slipped from A+ to A. Sawyer's grade rose to B+ and his card value climbed 80 percent. Suh's card value tripled. The roster that won CXLI is still good enough to win another; it simply ran into the coach who assembled it.

articles.headline: Champions, Then Sellers
articles.dek: Shareef London went to Tampa Bay for Shawn Milne, Jaclyde to Miami and Randall to Seattle before the second Atlanta season.
body: Shareef London's Atlanta chapter lasted one season. He arrived from the Bears in the Y83 multi-team trades, caught 91 passes for 1,579 yards, won the first ring of his career, and was then shipped to the Buccaneers for Shawn Milne before the second Falcons season. London leaves with 45 career touchdowns and a card value that rose 50 percent in his year as a Falcon.

He was not the only champion out the door. The MVP, Brandon Jaclyde, was traded to the Dolphins. Perrion Randall, an S-grade lineman after one season, was traded to the Seahawks, the club Skura's Jets beat in Super Bowls CXXXVI and CXXXIX.

What remains in Atlanta is the spine: Heath, Maxwell, Woodrum and the young defense of Otton, Fleming and Floyd, with Raimann at tight end. The coach has rebuilt on the fly before. He will have to do it again in year two.

articles.headline: Where the Old Jets Landed
articles.dek: Ty Lock found his footing with the Giants, Drake Wise posted 38 touchdowns in Baltimore and The Ox spent his first season as a Bear outside the playoffs.
body: Last offseason's trades scattered the Jets' stars around the league. One season later, the returns are in.

Ty Lock played 19 games for the Giants, a playoff appearance included, and threw for 3,678 yards and 33 touchdowns. The skill grades cooled on him slightly, from A+ to A-. Drake Wise, who passed through Atlanta on paper only, threw for 3,496 yards and 38 touchdowns for the Ravens in 19 games, and his card value rose 33 percent.

Kane Van Oxley had the quietest year of the three. "The Ox" played 17 games for the Bears with no postseason, catching 58 passes for 909 yards and 8 touchdowns. His skill grade slipped out of the S tier to A+.

That leaves the tackles chase as the league's headline pursuit. Dan Mosley's latest card holds 2,658 tackles, 204 behind Mose Junior's record.

The name to watch behind him is K'Lavon Settle. He added 238 tackles in 17 games, climbed to 2,356 for his career and moved up to an 89 overall with an A- grade. At that pace the tackles leaderboard will have a new name near the top within a few seasons.

The other side of the ledger belonged to two running backs who did not get a new card. JR Bashaam's value fell 46 percent as his OVR slid from 69 to 65, and Tramon Amerson's fell 42 percent with a drop from 71 to 68. Jake Gano, a defensive lineman, lost 22 percent.

seasonStories.tagline: A record season on the ground, a second straight title in Atlanta won with key pieces missing time, and two new names in the Hall of Fame.

articles.headline: Atlanta Does It Again
articles.dek: The Falcons went 13-3-1 and held off the Broncos 32-28 in Super Bowl CXLIII, carried by a record season from Ryland Maxwell and two first-year players who left with rings.
body: The Falcons are champions again. Atlanta finished the regular season 13-3-1, survived a four-point final against the Denver Broncos, 32-28 in Super Bowl CXLIII, and gave Dorren Skura a third straight title: one with the Jets, now two with the Falcons. A roster that was torn apart and rebuilt after the first ring simply did it again.

This one was won on the ground. Ryland Maxwell ran for 2,272 yards and 27 touchdowns, the best rushing season the record board has ever shown, and finished the job as Super Bowl MVP. He played all 20 games of the run and now owns 4 rings in 97 career games.

The passing game belonged to a newcomer. Orlando Larienne, in his first season, threw for 3,485 yards and 41 touchdowns and left with a ring. He appeared in only 15 of the 20 games, and a team that also saw Vyncint Heath miss time still found a way. Heath, the receiver they call "Starscream", caught 119 passes for 2,209 yards anyway and won a second Offensive Player of the Year award.

Up front, Calais Ham made 49 blocks in his first season and has a ring to show for it. Shawn Milne, who came from Tampa Bay in the trade that sent Shareef London the other way, won the first of his career, and Chance Woodrum now has 5.

Up the coast, the old club had a milestone of its own. Malakai Sawyer ran for 1,551 yards for the Jets and crossed into the Hall of Fame, and in Los Angeles the Rams' Von Horsted joined him in the same class. Two old warhorses went in. The Falcons kept winning.

articles.headline: Maxwell Runs Into the Record Book
articles.dek: 2,272 rushing yards in one season, a Super Bowl MVP and a fourth ring before his hundredth game.
body: No back on the record board had ever had a season like it. Ryland Maxwell carried the Falcons for 2,272 yards in Y84, the new mark for the best rushing season, and added 27 rushing touchdowns plus 4 more as a receiver. He did it in every one of Atlanta's 20 games, the one constant on a roster that had to cover for missing pieces elsewhere.

It was a jump even from the year he won Offensive Player of the Year, when he ran for 1,919. His career now reads 7,705 rushing yards and 102 rushing touchdowns in 97 games, and the season pushed him past 100 rushing scores.

The market noticed. His card rose from an overall of 67 to 75 and from a C+ grade to B+, and its value went from 20 to 112. With 4 rings and a Super Bowl MVP before his hundredth game, Maxwell has stopped being the back who followed the coach from New York. He is the reason Atlanta keeps winning.

articles.headline: A Title Won Short-Handed
articles.dek: Orlando Larienne played 15 of Atlanta's 20 games and Vyncint Heath played 18. The champions won anyway.
body: The Falcons' two most productive passing pieces were not always on the field. Orlando Larienne, a first-year quarterback, appeared in 15 of the club's 20 games, missing 5. Injury may have played a part; so may the usual caution with a newcomer on a new team. When he played, he was devastating: 41 touchdowns against 13 interceptions, better than three scores for every pick. His card opened in the A+ tier.

Vyncint Heath missed 2 games, a year after playing all 21 of Atlanta's first title run. Whether he was slowed by injury or simply by the wear of back-to-back deep seasons, the absence barely showed in the numbers. In 18 games he caught 119 passes for 2,209 yards and 22 touchdowns, 18.6 yards a catch, and took his second Offensive Player of the Year award. His card climbed into the S tier, its overall from 70 to 77.
Both finished with rings. For a team that had to keep winning with a starter or a star in street clothes, that may be the most telling number of all.

articles.headline: Green Bay Finds Its Back
articles.dek: Angelo Moton ran for 1,717 yards and 31 touchdowns and was named Rookie of the Year for the Packers.
body: Angelo Moton did not ease into the league. In his first 20 games for the Packers he ran for 1,717 yards and 31 touchdowns, and the Rookie of the Year award went to Green Bay. His 31 rushing scores matched what Malakai Sawyer, a new Hall of Famer, managed for the Jets in the same season.
There is one thing to clean up. Moton also put the ball on the ground more often than a back of his talent should, the kind of habit that decides playoff games.

He had help. Solomon Toohill played all 20 games at quarterback and threw for 3,845 yards and 41 touchdowns with 5 interceptions, his card rising from an overall of 66 to 70. Toohill already has a ring from Green Bay's 44-6 win over the Chiefs in Super Bowl CXXXVIII. With a back like this behind him, the Packers have reason to think about another.

articles.dek: A back who keeps running for the Jets and a Rams safety who never left Los Angeles both crossed Career Legacy 7,000.

Malakai Sawyer, in his second season back with the Jets, ran for 1,551 yards and 31 touchdowns in 19 games, passed 15,000 career rushing yards and reached a Career Legacy of 7,101. He has 16,436 rushing yards and 299 rushing touchdowns in 243 games, 2 rings and 2 Offensive Player of the Year awards.

Von Horsted got there one tackle at a time. A Ram since Y70 and nothing else, he played all 17 games, made 231 tackles, 13.6 a game, and intercepted 2 passes. That lifted his career to 2,658 tackles and 33 interceptions in 254 games and his Career Legacy from 6,833 to 7,345. His card's value rose from 3,118 to 4,806.
Sawyer's résumé is rings and records. Horsted's is a Defensive Player of the Year award and a body of work built entirely in one uniform. Neither has stopped.

articles.headline: The Jets Hand the Ball to a Rookie
articles.dek: Jimmy Tillery was intercepted only 4 times in his first season. Ty Lock, the old starter, is a Giant now.
body: The club Skura left behind went with youth at quarterback. Jimmy Tillery played all 19 of the Jets' games in his first season and threw for 3,392 yards and 27 touchdowns, with only 4 interceptions. He was not explosive, but he was careful, and careful kept the Jets in games.

He had a Hall of Famer behind him in Malakai Sawyer and a familiar target in Jaylen Conklin, the tight end they call "Takeoff", who caught 85 passes for 513 yards. Kalif Suh played all 19 games on defense.

Across town, Ty Lock is a Giant now, traded there from the Jets in the multi-team deal before Y83. He played 18 games and threw for 3,204 yards and 24 touchdowns with 2 interceptions. Lock owns 2 rings and 2 MVP awards. Tillery has a long way to go to match that, but the start was clean.

articles.headline: Life After Atlanta
articles.dek: Brandon Jaclyde, Shareef London and Perrion Randall left the champions after one season. All three spent Y84 watching their old club win again.
body: The Falcons traded away three pieces of their first title team, and none of them got a second ring. Brandon Jaclyde, the reigning Most Valuable Player, went to Miami and threw for 2,807 yards and 26 touchdowns with only 2 interceptions in 17 games for the Dolphins. Solid, but a long way from the 56 touchdowns he threw as a Falcon.

Shareef London's road ran from the Bears to Atlanta in the multi-team deal before Y83, then on to Tampa Bay in the trade for Shawn Milne. He caught 61 passes for 464 yards and 5 scores with the Buccaneers, 7.6 yards a catch. Milne, meanwhile, collected the ring.

Perrion Randall played 17 games for the Seahawks and was credited with 16 blocks. His card actually climbed, its overall from 66 to 74, even as his grade fell from the S tier to B+. For all three, Atlanta was a single season, a single ring, and then a view from somewhere else.

articles.headline: Denver Meets Skura, and Loses, Again
articles.dek: Four Super Bowls against the Broncos, four wins, with three different clubs across 68 seasons.
body: The Broncos have now reached the final against Dorren Skura four times and lost every one. The first came in Y16, a 22-16 win with the Commanders. Two more followed with the Buccaneers, 46-11 in Y23 and 38-16 in Y25. Then nothing for nearly six decades, until Atlanta beat Denver 32-28 in Super Bowl CXLIII.

This was the closest of the four by a distance. The first three were decided by six points or more, two of them by more than three touchdowns. Denver had a four-point game and a tight end with a long memory: D.C Paradis, who has 995 career catches, played all 20 games of the Broncos' run and is now five catches short of a thousand.
For Skura it is a rivalry measured in eras. The Commanders, the Buccaneers dynasty and now the Falcons have all taken their turn, and the Broncos are still waiting for their first win.

seasonStories.tagline: A fourth straight title for Dorren Skura, three records for Ryland Maxwell and a rookie Super Bowl MVP in Atlanta.

articles.headline: Four Straight for Skura, and Atlanta Has Never Looked Better
articles.dek: The Falcons went 15-2, beat the Bengals in Super Bowl CXLIV and gave Dorren Skura another title behind a record season from Ryland Maxwell.
body: The Falcons are champions for a third straight season, and Dorren Skura has now won four titles in a row across two clubs. Atlanta went 15-2 in the regular season, beat the Cincinnati Bengals in Super Bowl CXLIV and added another championship to Skura's career.

It was the most complete season of the run. The 15-2 mark was the club's best since Skura arrived, two wins better than last year's 13-3-1, and Atlanta played 20 games in all on the way to the trophy.

Ryland Maxwell was the engine again. He ran for 2,617 yards and 39 touchdowns, breaking his own single-season rushing mark and the rushing touchdown record on the same board, and added the best rushing game it has ever recorded, 237 yards. He won his second Offensive Player of the Year award and his fifth ring.

The new piece was a rookie. Apollo Adam caught 85 passes for 1,654 yards and 18 touchdowns in his first season and was named Super Bowl MVP. Orlando Larienne, who missed time a year ago, played in all 20 games and threw 51 touchdown passes. Vyncint Heath, the receiver they call "Starscream", added 2,059 yards.
Around the league, the Jets' Jimmy Tillery was named Most Valuable Player and Seattle's Deonte Sutton took Defensive Player of the Year. In Atlanta, the only question left is how long this can last.

articles.headline: Maxwell Breaks His Own Record, and Then Some
articles.dek: 2,617 rushing yards, 39 rushing touchdowns and a 237-yard game: Ryland Maxwell rewrote three lines of the record board in one season.
body: A year ago Ryland Maxwell set the best rushing season the record board had ever shown with 2,272 yards. In Y85 he cleared it by 345. He ran for 2,617 yards across all 20 of Atlanta's games, scored 39 rushing touchdowns to take a season record that had stood since Y38, and posted a 237-yard game that is now the best on the board.
That carried him past 10,000 career rushing yards. He now has 10,322 of them and 141 rushing touchdowns in 117 games, with 5 rings and 2 Offensive Player of the Year awards.

The market moved with him. His card went from an overall of 75 to 79 and from a B+ grade to A minus, and its value rose 150.9%, from 112 to 281. Two seasons ago he was a supporting piece who followed the coach from New York. Now the season rushing marks and the single-game yardage mark all carry his name.

body: Atlanta did not need a new star receiver. It found one anyway. Apollo Adam stepped into an offense that already had Vyncint Heath and averaged 19.5 yards a catch as a rookie: 85 receptions, 1,654 yards and 18 touchdowns.

He saved his best for the last game. Against the Bengals in Super Bowl CXLIV he was named Most Valuable Player, and he leaves his first season with a ring, a title-game award and a card that opened in the A tier.

He did it without playing every week. Adam appeared in 18 of Atlanta's 20 games, missing 2. Injury may have played a part, as may the usual care with a first-year player finding his place. The room had already changed: Shawn Milne, a champion in Atlanta in Y84, was traded to the Giants at the start of the season, and Heath carried the veteran load, playing all 20 games and catching 106 passes for 2,059 yards. The question now is not whether Adam belongs, but how much more there is.

articles.headline: Larienne Stays on the Field, and Atlanta Pulls Away
articles.dek: Orlando Larienne played all 20 games after missing 5 a year ago. This time Chance Woodrum, now with 6 rings, was the one who missed time.
body: Last season the Falcons won a title with their quarterback in and out of the lineup. This season Orlando Larienne was there for all 20 games, and the difference showed. He threw for 4,226 yards and 51 touchdowns and now has 92 touchdown passes in 35 career games, with 2 rings. The interceptions climbed too, 14 of them, the cost of a passing game built on big plays.
Vyncint Heath, who missed 2 games a year ago, also played every week this time.

The absence this year was in the secondary. Chance Woodrum appeared in 15 of the 20 games, missing 5. Injury may have been a factor; so may a lighter role in a deep defensive backfield. When he played he made 64 tackles and intercepted 3 passes, and he collected a sixth ring. A champion that kept its key pieces healthy for most of the year looked like a different team.

articles.headline: Record Watch: Settle Closes In on Junior
articles.dek: K'Lavon Settle made 208 tackles and sits 109 short of Mose Junior's 2,862. A new card, Juwann Gilman, is 10 behind him.
body: The career tackle mark still belongs to Mose Junior at 2,862, but the pack behind him tightened in Y85. Jayon Queen, the defensive back known as "FOV", remains closest at 2,838. The man moving fastest is K'Lavon Settle. The 49ers defensive back made 208 tackles in 17 games, 12.2 a game, and reached 2,753, 109 short. At this season's pace, one more year would do it.

Settle has company he did not have a year ago. Juwann Gilman of the Cardinals joined the card pool with 2,743 tackles, 32 interceptions, a Defensive Player of the Year award and a ring in 229 games. He opened with a Career Legacy of 7,557, enough to make him the only member of the Y85 Hall of Fame class, the first inducted under the higher bar.
In the backfield, Corey Ivey of the Ravens passed 20,000 career rushing yards and 350 rushing touchdowns in the same season. He has 362 scores, 26 short of Trequan Jensen's 388.

articles.headline: Old Hands, New Cards
articles.dek: Kahzin Heath in Denver, Camaron Knight and Juwann Gilman in Arizona and Linval Laulile in Pittsburgh joined the card pool with long careers already written.
body: Two quarterbacks with long resumes finally have cards. Kahzin Heath of the Broncos arrives with 40,614 passing yards and 398 touchdown passes in 235 games, against only 39 interceptions, plus a Rookie of the Year award and a Most Valuable Player award. What he does not have is a ring.

Camaron Knight of the Cardinals has the opposite profile. He has thrown fewer touchdowns, 359, for more yards, 42,351 in 246 games, but he has a ring and a Super Bowl MVP award. His card opened at an overall of 76, Heath's at 78.
Knight shares Arizona with Juwann Gilman, whose 2,743 tackles put him in the career record chase the moment his card was printed. Gilman also has a ring.

In Pittsburgh, Linval Laulile adds a Defensive Player of the Year award to 1,173 tackles and 14 interceptions in 110 games, 10.7 tackles a game. Four cards, three clubs, and years of football the market had never priced until now.

articles.headline: Tillery Takes the MVP in His Second Season
articles.dek: Jimmy Tillery threw for 4,183 yards and 44 touchdowns for the Jets, while Kalif Suh and Malakai Sawyer kept adding to long careers.
body: A year ago Jimmy Tillery was the careful rookie who kept the Jets in games. In Y85 he became the league's Most Valuable Player. Across 19 games he threw for 4,183 yards and 44 touchdowns with 6 interceptions, and added 5 more scores on the ground. His card's grade rose from C to B minus.

He had a familiar supporting cast. Jaylen Conklin, the tight end they call "Takeoff", caught 97 passes for 654 yards. Malakai Sawyer ran for 1,240 yards and 16 touchdowns and passed 300 career rushing touchdowns; he now has 315.

On defense, Kalif Suh played all 19 games, made 61 tackles and 2 sacks, and pushed his Career Legacy from 6,758 to 7,204. Suh has 3 rings, 20 career sacks and 10 forced fumbles in 192 games, and his card's value nearly doubled, from 1,070 to 2,016.
Ty Lock, the Jets' old starter, played 20 games for the Giants and threw 37 touchdown passes with 3 interceptions.

articles.headline: Cincinnati Joins the List
articles.dek: The Bengals have now met Dorren Skura in 3 Super Bowls and lost all 3, the first two to his Vikings.
body: Super Bowl CXLIV made the Bengals the latest club to learn what the Broncos learned a year earlier. Cincinnati reached the final, met Dorren Skura, and lost, just as it had in Y3 and Y68.

Those first two meetings came when Skura coached the Vikings. The Bengals lost Super Bowl LXII 30-22 and Super Bowl CXXVII 32-14, and then went the better part of two decades without seeing him in a final. This time he arrived with Atlanta, at the end of a 15-2 season, and the result did not change.

The final belonged to the Falcons' newest and oldest weapons. Apollo Adam, a rookie, was named the game's Most Valuable Player. Ryland Maxwell closed a season in which he broke three records. For Cincinnati, a franchise that has now been stopped by the same coach with two different clubs, the wait for a first win over Skura goes on.

articles.headline: Five Straight for Skura, and a Fourth in a Row for Atlanta
articles.dek: The Falcons went 13-4, beat the Bears, Eagles and Rams, then routed the Texans 48-13 in Super Bowl CXLV.
body: The Falcons are champions for a fourth straight season, and Dorren Skura has now won five titles in a row across two clubs. Atlanta finished the regular season 13-4, a step back from last year's 15-2, then beat the Chicago Bears, the Philadelphia Eagles and the Los Angeles Rams before taking apart the Houston Texans, 48-13, in Super Bowl CXLV.

This was the season Orlando Larienne took over the league. The quarterback threw for 4,821 yards and 50 touchdowns and was named Most Valuable Player for the first time. He did it while appearing in 19 of Atlanta's 21 games, missing 2, and Ryland Maxwell sat out the same number. Injury may have played a part for both, as may a long season's wear on the two players the offense leans on most. Neither looked slowed when it counted. Maxwell ran for 2,150 yards and 35 touchdowns and was named Super Bowl MVP for the second time in his career.

The passing game had a second engine. Apollo Adam, last year's Super Bowl MVP as a rookie, played every game, caught 114 passes for 2,200 yards and 22 touchdowns and was named Offensive Player of the Year. Vyncint Heath, the receiver they call "Starscream", added 2,027 yards and passed 10,000 for his career.

The rings kept stacking up. Chance Woodrum collected his seventh, Maxwell his sixth. Around the league, Kalif Suh of the Jets crossed into the Hall of Fame and K'Lavon Settle of the 49ers took over the career tackle lead. In Atlanta, four banners in four seasons have turned a new club into the standard everyone else is measured against.

articles.headline: Larienne Throws for 50 and Takes the MVP
articles.dek: Orlando Larienne threw 50 touchdown passes in 19 games and won the league's top individual award in his third season in Atlanta.
body: Two years ago Orlando Larienne was a newcomer who could not stay on the field. A year ago he played every game. This season he was the best player in the league. He threw for 4,821 yards, the most of his three seasons, and 50 touchdowns, and was named Most Valuable Player for the first time.

The price of the big plays was the same as ever. He threw 15 interceptions, a number Atlanta has learned to live with. He also did not play every week. Larienne appeared in 19 of the Falcons' 21 games, missing 2. Injury may have played a part; so may the care a contender takes with its most important player over a long season.

He now has 142 touchdown passes in 54 career games and 3 rings, one for every season he has been a Falcon. His card's overall rose from 62 to 67 and it kept its A+ grade. Few quarterbacks have done this much this quickly.

articles.headline: Maxwell Adds a Sixth Ring and a Second Super Bowl MVP
articles.dek: Ryland Maxwell ran for 2,150 yards and 35 touchdowns, then closed the season as the Most Valuable Player of Super Bowl CXLV.
body: Ryland Maxwell did not match the record season he put together a year ago. He did not need to. He ran for 2,150 yards and 35 touchdowns, 113.2 yards a game, and then saved his best for the final, where he was named Super Bowl MVP for the second time in his career.

He appeared in 19 of Atlanta's 21 games. Injury may have cost him the 2 he missed; so may the wear of carrying an offense for years. It did not show in the totals. He passed 150 career rushing touchdowns along the way and now has 176, with 12,472 rushing yards in 136 games and 6 rings.

The market moved with him again. His card's overall jumped from 79 to 87, its grade climbed from A minus to A, and its value rose 440.9%, from 281 to 1,520. The back who followed the coach from New York is now one of the most valuable cards in the league.

articles.headline: No Second-Year Slide: Adam Is Offensive Player of the Year
articles.dek: Apollo Adam caught 114 passes for 2,200 yards and 22 touchdowns and played all 21 of Atlanta's games.
body: A year after he was named Super Bowl MVP as a rookie, Apollo Adam became the centerpiece of the league's most dangerous passing game. He caught 114 passes for 2,200 yards and 22 touchdowns, 19.3 yards a catch, and was named Offensive Player of the Year. Unlike last season, when he missed time, he was on the field for every one of Atlanta's 21 games.
Through 39 career games he has 199 catches, 3,854 yards, 40 touchdowns and 2 rings. His card's overall rose from 62 to 68 and its grade from A to A+.

The veteran beside him had a milestone of his own. Vyncint Heath, "Starscream", caught 105 passes for 2,027 yards and 15 touchdowns, passing 10,000 career receiving yards and 100 receiving touchdowns in the same season. He now has 10,391 yards, 102 touchdowns and 5 rings. Defenses that rolled coverage toward one of them paid for it with the other.

articles.headline: Record Watch: Settle Takes the Career Tackle Lead
articles.dek: K'Lavon Settle made 212 tackles in 17 games and passed both Mose Junior and Jayon Queen. The mark is his at 2,965.
body: A year ago K'Lavon Settle sat 109 tackles behind Mose Junior's career mark. One more big season would do it, and he delivered. The 49ers defensive back made 212 tackles in 17 games, 12.5 a game, and finished with 2,965 for his career: 103 more than Junior's 2,862, and 127 more than the 2,838 of Jayon Queen, the defensive back known as "FOV". Every tackle from here adds to his own record.

The next man in line is Juwann Gilman of the Cardinals, at 2,743, 222 behind. The season also lifted Settle's Career Legacy from 7,028 to 7,392, which leaves him within one good year of the Hall of Fame.
Another mark is now within a single play. Kalif Suh of the Jets has 10 forced fumbles, 1 behind Tyrone Baugh's 11.

articles.headline: Suh Crosses the Bar as the Jets' Core Keeps Producing
articles.dek: Kalif Suh's Career Legacy reached 7,503, making him the Y86 Hall of Fame class, and Jimmy Tillery threw 31 touchdown passes without an interception.
body: Kalif Suh did not need a spectacular season to reach the Hall of Fame. He needed a steady one. The Jets linebacker played 18 games, made 66 tackles and pushed his Career Legacy from 7,204 to 7,503, just enough to clear the bar and stand alone as the Y86 class.
His line across 210 games reads 638 tackles, 17 interceptions, 20 sacks and 10 forced fumbles, with 3 rings from Skura's Jets teams in Y77, Y80 and Y82. When the coach left for Atlanta, Suh stayed.

The rest of the Jets' core kept producing. Jimmy Tillery, last year's Most Valuable Player, threw for 3,532 yards and 31 touchdowns in 18 games without a single interception. Malakai Sawyer ran for 1,453 yards and 26 touchdowns and passed 19,000 career rushing yards. Jaylen Conklin, the tight end they call "Takeoff", caught 91 passes. New York did not reach the final, but the old guard is still there.

articles.headline: Atlanta Reloads: Saine and Clapp Arrive, Woodrum Adds a Seventh
articles.dek: Two first-year Falcons won rings, Simeon Otton collected his fourth and Calais Ham kept the line in order.
body: Every champion loses pieces, and the Falcons keep finding new ones. Marc Saine II, a tight end new to the card pool, caught 53 passes for 730 yards and 10 touchdowns in 21 games, a score every 5.3 catches, and his card opened with an A minus grade. Ian Clapp, a defensive back, made 141 tackles and intercepted 2 passes in 19 games, 7.4 tackles a game. He was absent for 2 of Atlanta's games; injury may have been a factor, as may the time a newcomer needs to earn every snap.

The veterans held their places. Chance Woodrum played all 21 games, made 148 tackles and won his seventh ring. Simeon Otton, on the Falcons' defense since Y83, made 86 tackles and 4 sacks, and has won a ring in every one of those seasons, 4 in all; his grade rose from B to A minus. Calais Ham made 68 blocks and now owns 3 rings in 61 career games, with an S grade on his card.

articles.headline: Houston Gets Its Second Look at Skura, and the Same Ending
articles.dek: The Texans lost Super Bowl CXLV 48-13. Their only other final against Dorren Skura, in Y38, ended the same way.
body: The Houston Texans waited a long time for another shot at Dorren Skura in a Super Bowl. Their only previous meeting came in Y38, when Skura coached the Seattle Seahawks and won Super Bowl XCVII 24-16. That one was close. This one, 48-13, was not.

Atlanta's road ran through three playoff wins, over the Chicago Bears, the Philadelphia Eagles and the Los Angeles Rams. The Rams had one of the league's most productive backs in Tim Wright, who ran for 1,418 yards and 25 touchdowns in 19 games before their season ended against the champions.

For Houston, the defeat joins a short and painful list. The Texans also lost Super Bowl CXXXII in Y73, 41-40 to the Arizona Cardinals, a final Skura had no part in. Three trips to the last game, three losses, two of them to the same coach with two different clubs. The franchise is still looking for its first title.
